entry.title: The Developer’s AI Journey: From Prompts to AI-Native Engineering

link.title: The Developer’s AI Journey: From Prompts to AI-Native Engineering

entry.content:
OPEN MIND · INQUIRY · ENGINEERING · XXI → 0

There has never been so much AI within a developer's reach—and perhaps never so much uncertainty about where to begin.

One day we are discovering autocomplete. Soon we are debating prompts, vibe coding, context windows, agentic workflows, MCP, Skills, AI-driven delivery, and AI-native systems. Every week offers another tool, another framework, another claim that everything has changed.

What does a developer actually need to learn? And more importantly, what is changing in the way we understand and build software?

The journey is not about mastering AI. It is about transforming understanding.

Contents

  • A map, not a maturity ladder
  • Three paths through the journey
  • Act I — The Awakening
  • Act II — The Turning Point
  • Act III — Integration and Return
  • The 22 Major Arcana as three interwoven paths
  • A practical engineering example
  • Where are you in the journey?
  • XXI → 0: the return
  • The Journey as a Semantic Model
  • References and further reading

A map, not a maturity ladder

The Fool’s Journey, a popular narrative interpretation of the 22 Major Arcana, gives us an intriguing metaphor. The Fool (0) represents openness: the willingness to step forward without possessing every answer. The World (XXI) represents integration: seeing connections that were invisible at the beginning. But the story does not end there. XXI returns to 0. Experience changes the traveler; uncertainty remains.

This is a literary and educational metaphor, not a claim that tarot predicts technological progress. Nor is it a prescription that every developer must encounter every tool in the same order. Different capabilities overlap; they are not badges on a universal career ladder.

The central question

Instead of asking “Which tool comes after prompts?”, ask “What problem am I trying to understand, and what capability would help me investigate it responsibly?”

Major Arcana imagery: Rider–Waite–Smith (Pam-A) collection, illustrated by Pamela Colman Smith (1909–1910), via Wikimedia Commons. Original artwork is public domain; card images load from Wikimedia Commons and require an internet connection unless downloaded locally.

Three paths through the journey

The Secret of the Sphinx explores a symbolic reading of three paths: Osiris, Thoth–Sopdet, and Horus. We can borrow that interpretive lens for software engineering without suggesting that it is an established historical taxonomy of tarot or a mandated order of technological progress.

These are three interwoven paths with specific Arcana sequences, not three compulsory levels. Transformation challenges assumptions; awakening deepens observation and understanding; experience tests understanding through action. Their symbolic lessons can overlap in practice, but the card sequences shown below retain their defined order.

PATH I

Osiris · Transformation

What must I reconsider or leave behind?

From the assumption that productivity means typing code, to questioning premature trust, obsolete habits, and fragile automation.

Developer practice: review assumptions, recognize failure modes, and redesign the process.

PATH II

Thoth–Sopdet · Awakening

What am I beginning to understand?

Prompts, context, tools, MCP, agents, and Skills expand what can be explored—but do not automatically establish what is true.

Developer practice: investigate, ask better questions, and make uncertainty explicit.

PATH III

Horus · Experience

How can I apply and validate what I understand?

Turn hypotheses into bounded workflows, useful software, tests, reviews, evaluations, and accountable AI-native design.

Developer practice: build, measure, verify, and learn from consequences.

0 · Open mind→ Transformation · Awakening · Experience→ XXI · Integration↻ 0 · Renewed inquiry

Three paths, one evolving understanding. Transformation changes our assumptions. Awakening changes what we notice. Experience tests what we build. None of them removes the need for the others.

The arcana remain the symbolic encounters of the story; these paths describe different ways to interpret what happens during those encounters. For example, the Hanged Man (XII) belongs to the Path of Horus, the Tower (XVI) to the Path of Osiris, and Justice (XI) to the Path of Thoth–Sopdet. These correspondences are editorial interpretations rather than fixed tarot rules.

Act I — The Awakening

Explore Arcana 0–IVOpen mind, code completion, prompts, creativity and workflows
ARCANUM 0

The Fool — An open mind

Imagine a developer in a familiar environment: editor, terminal, tests, pull requests, deadlines. A new assistant appears in the IDE. Curiosity competes with skepticism: Will this help? Will I lose my skills? Should I trust it?

An open mind is not unconditional enthusiasm. It is the willingness to experiment without surrendering judgment. The first change is not in the stack; it is in the posture toward the unknown.

ARCANUM I

The Magician — Code completion

An intelligently suggested line, a function, a test scaffold: the developer still chooses the direction, while AI reduces friction at the keyboard.

The small convenience raises a much larger question: If AI can complete code, what else could it help me do?

ARCANUM II

The High Priestess — Prompts and context

Conversation expands beyond completion: explain an unfamiliar Rails service, surface trade-offs, compare approaches, or challenge an assumption.

Strong prompting depends on context, constraints, examples, and iterative inquiry—not magical wording or presumed correctness.

ARCANUM III

The Empress — Vibe coding and creation

Natural-language generation accelerates prototypes. An idea becomes an interface or small product quickly enough to discover what the developer actually wants.

But vibe coding, especially without serious code inspection, is not the same as production-grade engineering. Demonstrating possibility is not proving reliability.

ARCANUM IV

The Emperor — Workflows and structure

Instead of collecting disconnected answers, turn work into a reproducible sequence: research, design, implement, test, review, publish. Make inputs, checks, and outputs explicit.

The emphasis shifts from one useful answer to a dependable way of working.

WEAK REQUEST

“Refactor this job.”

ENGINEERING REQUEST

“Identify failure modes in this Sidekiq job, preserve idempotency, propose alternatives, and show which assumptions require tests.”

Act II — The Turning Point

Explore Arcana V–XVISkills, tools, agency, verification, perspective and risks
ARCANUM V

The Hierophant — Skills and tradition

Expertise can be captured in reusable Skills: procedures, project conventions, examples, review criteria, and domain knowledge.

The question changes from What should I prompt? to Which practice can my team repeat and inspect?

ARCANUM VI

The Lovers — Human–AI collaboration

AI can propose and execute. The developer still frames intent, defines boundaries, evaluates trade-offs, and accepts responsibility.

Good collaboration is neither total delegation nor refusal to delegate; it is a deliberate division of work.

ARCANUM VII

The Chariot — Tools and MCP

Tools expose concrete actions; MCP provides a protocol for connecting approved capabilities and context. An assistant can reach repositories, APIs, documentation, and tests.

Access expands what can be done, but permissions and provenance must remain explicit.

Tools / MCPAccess to systems and actions
AgentsPlanning and multistep execution
SkillsReusable ways of doing work
VerificationEvidence that results meet expectations
ARCANUM VIII

Strength — Controlled autonomy

Agents can plan and perform multistep work, including editing files, running checks, and proposing a pull request.

Controlled autonomy requires bounded goals, permissions, traceability, checkpoints, and human approval where warranted.

ARCANUM IX

The Hermit — Reflection and discernment

When a result looks convincing, the developer must still ask: How do I know?

Reflection means examining assumptions, reading the code, reviewing generated explanations, and seeking evidence beyond fluent output.

ARCANUM X

Wheel of Fortune — A changing landscape

Models, products, and workflows evolve. What works today may change with the next release or context window.

Keep the engineering principles portable: explicit requirements, reproducible tests, observability, and the ability to recover safely.

ARCANUM XI

Justice — Verification and accountability

A passing test does not necessarily prove the right behavior was tested. A link does not automatically supply evidence. A successful tool call is not a validated business outcome.

Verification joins correctness, security, provenance, and accountable review. Capability is not correctness.

ARCANUM XII

The Hanged Man — A change in perspective

This is the turning point: producing more code faster is not the same as knowing what should be built, why, and how to determine whether it fulfills the intent.

Code becomes an expression of understanding, never its substitute.

ARCANUM XIII

Death — Letting go of assumptions

Some assumptions must be released: that professional value is measured by lines typed, that every task needs an agent, or that a demo proves readiness.

Leaving those assumptions behind makes more room for domain understanding and sound engineering choices.

ARCANUM XIV

Temperance — Human–AI integration

Balance automation with tests, architecture, observability, human communication, and operational constraints.

The goal is not to choose human or machine, but to design a process in which each contributes what can be justified and verified.

ARCANUM XV

The Devil — The dependency trap

Convenience can become dependence: unfamiliar code is accepted, investigation is skipped, and authority is delegated without safeguards.

The danger is less the presence of AI than the disappearance of independent judgment.

ARCANUM XVI

The Tower — Failure reveals the architecture

Reality intervenes: a payment job retries twice, a data migration violates invariants, or an agent changes the wrong files.

Failure asks a sharper question: What did our process fail to understand?

Capability is not correctness.

AI can generate options. Engineering judgment evaluates constraints, evidence, risks, and consequences.

Act III — Integration and Return

Explore Arcana XVII–XXINew perspectives, uncertainty, clarity and AI-native integration
ARCANUM XVII

The Star — Renewed vision

A renewed engineering vision sees relationships among people, knowledge, tools, models, policies, and evaluations.

We can pursue better outcomes rather than simply more generated output.

ARCANUM XVIII

The Moon — Uncertainty and evidence

Models generate claims; systems retrieve sources; neither operation proves understanding. Uncertainty must be represented rather than concealed.

Distinguish output, source, evidence, claim, and understanding, and keep unresolved questions visible.

ARCANUM XIX

The Sun — Clarity through inquiry

Clarity grows when intent is explicit and observations can be tested against expectations.

The objective is not certainty about everything. It is an honest, revisable account of what the system does and why.

ARCANUM XX

Judgement — Reimagining architecture

The architectural question emerges: when should AI participate in a running product rather than only in the development workflow?

Think about model inference, tools, context, evaluation, governed actions, and feedback as designed capabilities—not magic defaults.

ARCANUM XXI

The World — Integration, not completion

A wider picture comes into view. Prompts, Skills, agents, workflows, and models become design choices in service of people and real constraints.

The World is integration, not final mastery. From XXI the developer returns to 0—with fresh questions and a wider perspective.

DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE

AI-Assisted

AI helps developers build.

Example: GitHub Copilot suggests Rails code, explains a service, or drafts a test for human review.

ENGINEERING WORKFLOW

AI-Driven

AI drives bounded parts of the process.

Example: An agent proposes a change, runs tests, and prepares a pull request for human approval.

PRODUCT ARCHITECTURE

AI-Native

AI participates in the running system.

Example: A product integrates model inference, tools, context, evaluation, and governed actions.

These are working distinctions, not an official certification ladder. An AI-native product can still be developed with traditional tooling; an AI-assisted team can ship entirely deterministic software.

The 22 Major Arcana as three interwoven paths

The card associations below are interpretive, not technological milestones. Begin with 0 — The Fool above, then expand any of the three paths to explore its seven-card sequence as illustrated cards with engineering context. The final card, XXI — The World, returns to 0. We use the common Rider–Waite–Smith numbering, where Strength is VIII and Justice is XI.

Card artwork: Pamela Colman Smith, Rider–Waite–Smith tarot (1909). Public-domain originals. Images are currently served from an external archive; use the included download script to self-host them before publishing.

Follow each path in its own order: Osiris · Thoth–Sopdet · Horus. The cards are deliberately interwoven, not consecutive phases.

The Path of Osiris — TransformationI → IV → VII → X → XIII → XVI → XIXWhat must I reconsider or leave behind?

ARCANA X

ARCANA XIII

ARCANA XVI

ARCANA XIX

The Path of Thoth–Sopdet — AwakeningII → V → VIII → XI → XIV → XVII → XXWhat am I beginning to understand?
ARCANA II

ARCANA V

ARCANA VIII

ARCANA XI

ARCANA III

ARCANA VI

ARCANA IX

ARCANA XII

ARCANA XV

ARCANA XVIII

ARCANA XXI

The World

Integrated Engineering

Connecting the whole and returning to renewed inquiry

A practical engineering example

Suppose you are asked to improve the reliability of payment processing in a Rails application.

An autocomplete-only approach helps write another retry method. A prompt-first approach asks for recommendations. A workflow-driven approach inspects the code, develops a failure model, implements changes, runs checks, and requires review. With tools and agents, much of that work can be coordinated across repository, CI, and documentation. With Skills, project-specific conventions can become repeatable.

But none of those capabilities can replace the critical questions: Is the operation idempotent? What happens under duplicate delivery? Which side effects can be reversed? Which invariant proves business correctness? Who approves the change?

OUTPUT-CENTRIC

“The AI wrote a retry policy.”

UNDERSTANDING-CENTRIC

“We identified the failure modes, tested the invariants, and can explain why the recovery policy is appropriate.”

The deepest gain is not the number of generated lines. It is the ability to discover, test, and preserve a more accurate account of the system.

Where are you in the journey?

Do not measure your progress by how many new products you have installed. Ask which questions you can now answer:

  • Exploring? Can you explain what you want AI to help you discover?
  • Prompting? Can you supply context, constraints, and verification criteria?
  • Automating? Can your workflow fail visibly and recover safely?
  • Connecting tools? Can you describe what the system is permitted to access and change?
  • Delegating to agents? Can you tell the difference between execution success and task correctness?
  • Designing AI-native systems? Can you represent uncertainty, audit decisions, and evaluate outcomes?
Compass, not checklist

Find your current question. Choose the smallest capability that helps answer it. Verify what you learned. Repeat.

ARCANA XXI

The World

Integrated Engineering

Connecting the whole and returning to renewed inquiry

→
ARCANA 0

The Fool

Open Mind

Curiosity and willingness to explore the unknown

A New Understanding. A New Beginning.

XXI → 0: the return

The Fool begins without knowing. The World arrives with a wider understanding. But wisdom is not the absence of uncertainty. It is the ability to return to uncertainty with better questions, stronger methods, and greater responsibility.

The engineer who first discovered intelligent autocomplete is not quite the same engineer who now considers agent orchestration, Skills, evidence, or AI-native architecture. Yet the most important capability remains recognizable: an open mind prepared to investigate what is actually happening.

Every new tool expands what a developer can do. Every new understanding transforms what a developer can become.

The World is not the end of the journey. It is the moment the Fool discovers a new beginning.

The Journey as a Semantic Model

The twenty-two Arcana can be described once as a set of contextual meanings, then related through three interwoven paths. In this interpretation, Context situates each card in AI engineering, Light expresses its constructive possibility, Shadow explores its limitations, and Insight captures a question or understanding that may emerge. These are interpretive perspectives, not proven properties of the cards or evidence about AI systems.

The Mermaid diagram presents the overall relationships. Expand the Ruby DSL below to explore the full model of the 22 Arcana, their AI contexts, three paths, and the return XXI → 0. This is an illustrative Ruby DSL, not a working parser or executable implementation.

The journey does not repeat itself. It unfolds again from a different understanding.

entry.title: From Ericsson Use Cases to AI-Native Systems

link.title: From Ericsson Use Cases to AI-Native Systems

entry.content:
The use case is the boundary that transforms human intention into a distributed AI architecture.

Contents

  • The AI-Native question
  • Ivar Jacobson and Ericsson
  • AXE, PLEX and Function Blocks
  • HLPLEX, processes and FORLOPP
  • From Ericsson languages to concurrent systems
  • From function blocks to AI building blocks
  • One use case, decomposed end to end
  • The use case as an AI boundary
  • When context becomes a layer above the function
  • Conclusion

The AI-Native question

The AI industry often presents intention-driven systems as something entirely new. But an AI-Native system does not simply receive an intention and autonomously invent the entire solution.

It must understand what the intention means, determine what the system is responsible for, identify the participating actors, decompose the business process and select the appropriate capabilities.

The real starting point is not the agent.

It is the use case.

Actor
  → Intent
    → Use Case
      → Business Process
        → Responsibilities
          → AI Building Blocks
            → Outcome

The use case turns an intention into a bounded responsibility. It tells the system who participates, what must happen, what is allowed, what is outside the boundary, what counts as success and what evidence must be produced.

A requirement states what should happen. A use case defines the bounded process through which it can happen.

Ivar Jacobson and Ericsson

Before use cases became widely associated with UML, Objectory and the Rational Unified Process, Ivar Jacobson was working at Ericsson on large, real-time telecom systems such as AKE and AXE, including PLEX.

Jacobson is widely credited with introducing use cases in 1986 as a way to specify functional software requirements. The idea emerged from a practical problem: how to understand systems whose behaviour was distributed across software units, processes, signals and hardware.

The historical connection matters because the use case was not created as a decorative documentation technique. It was a way to reason about responsibility:

Who interacts with the system?
What does the actor need to accomplish?
What functions are required?
Where does each responsibility live?
How do the units cooperate?

AXE, PLEX and Function Blocks

The AXE system gives this history a concrete form. PLEX-C was used to produce software for the central processor of the AXE control system. Functional blocks could also involve hardware and regional software running in regional processors.

This meant that a system function was not necessarily located in one place:

Central Software
  + Regional Software
    + Hardware
      + Functional Blocks
        + Signals

The conceptual decomposition was:

Actor
  → Use Case
    → System Function
      → Function Block
        → Software Unit
          → Process
            → Signal / Event

A Function Block was not simply a source-code file. It represented a function within a larger application system, potentially combining software, local data, signal interfaces, associated hardware and regional software.

Legend: the Function Block is the unit of composition within the application system; it brings together software, data, interfaces and physical or regional resources.

The use case gave the function its reason for existing. The Function Block gave the function an architectural home.

HLPLEX, processes and FORLOPP

HLPLEX made active execution and concurrency more explicit. Modules could contain processes; processes could execute concurrently, have multiple instances and communicate through event paths.

Function Block
  └── Module
       ├── Process A
       ├── Process B
       └── Process C

Process A
  → Event
    → Process B

The unit was no longer only a container of functionality. It became an active participant in a larger process.

The AXE documentation also describes FORLOPP as a sequence of events. When multiple Function Blocks participated in the same call, records could be linked into a chain with a Forlopp Identity, or FID.

Call
  → Record in Block A
    → Record in Block B
      → Record in Block C
        → Record in Block D

FID = identity of the distributed call

The FID allowed the system to identify and release a specific call in the event of a software failure. This is not identical to a modern trace ID or agent run ID, but the architectural question is related:

How does one preserve the identity of an operation while it crosses multiple units?

From Ericsson languages to concurrent systems

The historical arc can be read as:

PLEX
  → HLPLEX
    → Erlang
      → Elixir

This should not be understood as a direct succession of compilers or language versions. PLEX and HLPLEX were Ericsson languages and execution environments for telecom systems; Erlang emerged later from the same Ericsson context and addressed related problems at a broader level.

The important continuity is architectural:

PLEX / HLPLEX
  → Function Blocks
  → Processes
  → Events and Signals
  → Distributed Execution

Erlang / Elixir
  → Processes
  → Message Passing
  → Isolation
  → Supervision
  → Fault Tolerance

Erlang and Elixir therefore belong to a longer Ericsson tradition of decomposing complex systems into interacting, concurrent and recoverable units. The lineage is not only syntactic. It is a lineage of architectural concerns: decomposition, communication, concurrency, isolation, supervision and composition.

AI-Native systems extend this lineage with another layer:

Distributed Execution
  → Intent
    → Context
      → Adaptive Feedback

The function is still distributed, but its participation can now be directed by an intention and the context in which that intention is being pursued.

From function blocks to AI building blocks

The history of software paradigms is also a history of changing answers to one question:

What is the right unit for realizing a responsibility?

OOP
  → Object = data + behaviour

PLEX
  → Function Block = function + software + hardware

HLPLEX
  → Process = state + behaviour + events

Erlang / Elixir
  → Process = isolation + messages + supervision

Ruby / Ractors
  → Unit = isolation + parallel execution

AI-Native
  → Agent = state + behaviour + intent + feedback

The paradigms are not identical and do not form a simple chain of direct inheritance. They respond to related pressures: decomposition, encapsulation, communication, concurrency, recovery, composition and responsibility.

An AI-Native system is not composed only of agents. It is composed of different building blocks, each with a distinct role:

Responsibility Building block
Specialized knowledge Skill / RAG
Concrete execution Tool
External integration MCP
Known sequence Workflow
Adaptive judgment Agent
Persistent context Memory
Lifecycle control Hook
Sensitive authorization Human actor

The use case determines which of these are necessary.

One use case, decomposed end to end

Begin with a bounded objective:

🧭 INTENT

Investigate a production incident and produce a verified report.

Before decomposing this intention into AI building blocks, we can express it as a classic use case: an authorized engineer interacts with an incident-investigation system to obtain a verified report and, when necessary, approve a risky change.

Legend: the use case diagram identifies the actor, the system boundary, the goal and the controlled extension requiring authorization.

This is not yet an architecture. We first turn it into a bounded use case:

An authorized engineer requests an investigation. The system gathers relevant documentation and telemetry, forms and tests hypotheses, records evidence, produces a report and requests human approval before any risky production change.

The use case diagram defines the goal and the system boundary. The sequence below shows how that goal is realized over time, with context directing which capabilities participate at each stage.

Legend: the sequence shows context as an active participant in execution, not merely as information loaded before the agent starts.

The distributed business process becomes visible:

Incident Investigation
  ├── receive the request
  ├── identify the affected service
  ├── retrieve relevant documentation
  ├── inspect logs and metrics
  ├── form hypotheses
  ├── run safe verification steps
  ├── evaluate evidence
  ├── produce a report
  └── request approval for risky action

Each responsibility can now be assigned to an appropriate participant:

Receive and classify request       → Coordinator Agent
Retrieve runbooks and documentation → RAG
Apply incident procedure           → Skill
Query logs and metrics             → Tool
Connect to observability systems   → MCP
Compare hypotheses                 → Investigation Agent
Execute standard checks            → Workflow
Preserve findings and context      → Memory
Block unsafe operations            → Hook / Policy
Approve production changes         → Human Actor

Legend: the diagram separates context, execution and governance; the use case routes the intention through bounded capabilities toward evidence and human-verified completion.

The diagram does not show one super-agent performing everything. It shows a distributed process in which each building block has a bounded responsibility.

The use case as an AI boundary

The use case is the boundary that transforms intention into AI architecture:

Use Case
  → defines purpose
    → assigns responsibility
      → restricts authority
        → selects building blocks
          → defines completion

For every agent, skill, tool or workflow, we should be able to ask:

Which use case requires this?
Which responsibility does it realize?
What authority does it have?
What does it communicate?
What evidence does it produce?
When must it stop?

This prevents common category errors:

Agent ≠ Skill
Skill ≠ Tool
Tool ≠ MCP
MCP ≠ RAG
RAG ≠ Memory
Hook ≠ Workflow

Not every responsibility needs to become an agent. Not every capability needs autonomy. Not every document needs to become memory. Not every integration needs to become an MCP server.

The use case must decide.

Intention should not be confused with a prompt. A prompt is one possible interface to an AI model; an intention is the human or business purpose that gives the system direction.

Intention ≠ Prompt
Intention → Use Case → Context → AI Execution

The use case also defines what must not happen: actions outside the scope, capabilities without authority, data that cannot be used, decisions that require human approval and conditions under which execution must stop. This negative space is part of the architecture.

When context becomes a layer above the function

In a traditional distributed system, the main architectural question was often where a function should execute:

Use Case
  → System Function
    → Function Block
      → Process
        → Signal

In an AI-Native system, the functions still exist, but a contextual layer helps decide which ones should participate in the current situation:

Intent
  → Use Case
    → Context
      → Responsibilities
        → Functions and AI Building Blocks
          → Action and Evidence

Consider the same production incident under two different contexts:

Context Directed execution
A service is degraded, but no data loss is detected Retrieve runbooks, inspect metrics and perform safe diagnostics
The same service shows possible data corruption Retrieve recovery procedures, increase evidence requirements and require human approval before changes

The underlying functions may be similar, but the context changes their order, authority and level of caution. In the first situation, a diagnostic workflow may be enough. In the second, the system may need additional RAG sources, a specialized skill, an investigation agent, stronger hooks and a human checkpoint.

This is the additional layer introduced by AI-Native systems:

Function = what can be done
Context  = what matters now
Use Case = why it is being done and where it must stop

The use case therefore does not replace the distributed function. It gives direction to the function through context, throughout execution.

In this sense, intention becomes an architectural input:

Intent
  → Use Case
    → Context
      → System Boundary
        → Responsibilities
          → AI Building Blocks

The use case is the bridge between human intention and system design. It turns intention into a bounded context in which AI can reason, act, produce evidence and stop.

Conclusion

The history of software composition can be read as a history of changing units:

Object
  → Function Block
    → Process
      → Supervised Application
        → Ractor
          → Agent

Each unit addressed a different aspect of complexity:

Object           → encapsulation
Function Block   → functional composition
Process          → active execution
Message          → communication
Supervision      → recovery
Ractor           → isolation and parallelism
Agent            → intention and adaptive action

But the unit alone is never enough. A system also needs purpose, responsibility, authority, context, constraints, evidence and completion.

The use case provides that definition. It is where a human intention becomes a system responsibility, where a business process becomes an architectural boundary and where the system decides what belongs inside the solution and what must remain outside it.

📄 TAKEAWAY

AI-Native systems do not begin with agents. They begin with intentions that become use cases, use cases that become responsibilities, and responsibilities that become carefully chosen building blocks.

The use case is where intention becomes architecture. It does not remove the need for system modeling; it gives system modeling a more direct starting point.

References

  • Ivar Jacobson — biography and work
  • Ivar Jacobson International
  • Object Management Group — UML
  • Ruby Ractor documentation
  • Model Context Protocol
  • Google Cloud — Agentic AI security operations workflow

The AXE, PLEX and HLPLEX historical details in this article were checked against Ericsson training manuals supplied as research material. The article paraphrases those materials and does not reproduce their proprietary diagrams or code.

entry.title: Beyond the Sphinx — Architecture for Deep Time

link.title: Beyond the Sphinx — Architecture for Deep Time

entry.content:
To researchers, archaeologists, and independent thinkers who keep exploring Egypt with rigor and imagination — reminding us that the past is not a closed book, but a deeper conversation with time.

Perhaps the mystery is not what Egypt wanted to tell us, but why it built as if time itself were part of the audience.

Some monuments are made for a generation.

Others are made for a dynasty.

And then there are structures whose scale, material and mass seem to belong to a different category altogether: architecture that can survive the disappearance of the people who built it.

The pyramids of Giza are still here after roughly four and a half millennia. The Osireion at Abydos still holds its monumental stone architecture below ground. At Hawara, little remains above the surface of the temple complex that ancient authors called the Labyrinth, yet archaeology and geophysics continue to recover traces of what once stood there.

This article begins where The Secret of the Sphinx ended.

That earlier journey asked whether the Sphinx and pyramids could be read symbolically as a compass carried across civilizational cycles.

Here the question is different.

Why build for deep time at all?

And if Egypt’s monumental architecture was deliberately made to endure, what are we still failing to understand about it?

At a Glance

This article follows five layers:

  1. What is confirmed — spaces and structures established through archaeology or reproducible measurement.
  2. What remains unknown — features whose purpose or full extent is still unresolved.
  3. What is claimed — recent interpretations that have not yet received independent archaeological confirmation.
  4. What is remembered — ancient descriptions such as the Labyrinth at Hawara and Egypt’s own language of primordial order.
  5. What the architecture suggests philosophically — not a hidden message asserted as fact, but a question about permanence, memory and time.

The distinction matters.

A mystery becomes more interesting, not less, when we know exactly where the evidence ends.

Evidence Key

🟢 Confirmed — supported by archaeology, direct observation or reproducible measurement.
🟡 Historical — preserved in ancient texts, excavation records or documented tradition, but not necessarily fully reconstructed.
🟣 Interpretive — a symbolic, ritual or initiatory reading that goes beyond what archaeology alone can establish.
🔵 Esoteric / visionary — material from psychic, occult or revelatory traditions, presented as such rather than as archaeological evidence.

The same monument may appear in more than one layer. The label tells us what kind of claim is being made, not whether the subject is worth exploring.

Three sites, three open questions

  • Great Pyramid

    Established: internal spaces, including a muon-detected void and an imaged corridor.

    Open question: the purpose of these features.

  • Osireion

    Established: a monumental subterranean structure associated archaeologically with Seti I's complex.

    Open question: how to understand its unusual form and symbolism.

  • Hawara

    Established: Amenemhat III's temple complex is identified with the Labyrinth tradition.

    Open question: the complex's original form, extent and surviving remains.

Contents

  • From Legacy to Permanence
  • Architecture for Deep Time
  • The Pyramid Is Still Not Fully Known
  • Beneath Giza: Signal Is Not Structure
  • The Osireion: Architecture Below Time
  • Hawara and the Memory of the Labyrinth
  • The Initiatory Geography Hypothesis
  • Edgar Cayce and the Hall of Records
  • Before Egypt Was Egypt
  • Atlantis: Answer or Archetype?
  • Built to Cross Ages
  • Time as the Audience
  • What Have We Not Yet Learned to Read?
  • As Before, So After
  • References and Further Reading

From Legacy to Permanence

The previous article explored the possibility of a legacy intended for future humanity.

This time we do not begin with the message.

We begin with the medium.

Stone.

Not a tablet that can be carried away. Not a manuscript dependent on language. Not an institution dependent on political continuity.

A mountain of engineered stone.

That changes the question.

Why choose a medium whose useful lifetime exceeds the civilization that produced it?

The conventional archaeological answers remain essential. Egyptian monumental architecture expressed royal power, funerary belief, cult, cosmic order and the transformation of the king. None of that needs to be discarded.

But permanence itself deserves attention.

A monument may communicate through inscriptions.

A megalithic monument also communicates through its continued existence.

Architecture for Deep Time

“Deep time” is normally a geological idea: a scale so large that an individual human life becomes almost negligible.

Megalithic architecture creates something analogous in culture.

A person dies.

A dynasty ends.

A language changes.

A religion transforms.

The stone remains.

This does not prove that the builders intended to address people thousands of years in the future.

But it establishes something simpler and observable:

the architecture was capable of doing so.

That capacity becomes part of the monument’s historical afterlife.

The Pyramid Is Still Not Fully Known

The Great Pyramid is one of the most studied buildings on Earth.

It still surprises us.

In 2017, the ScanPyramids collaboration reported the detection of a previously unknown large void above the Grand Gallery using cosmic-ray muography. The signal was independently observed with three detector systems. The feature, known as the ScanPyramids Big Void, has a minimum length of about 30 metres. Its purpose remains unknown.

That distinction is crucial:

existence: strongly supported.

function: unknown.

In 2023 a corridor behind the chevron-shaped stones on the north face of the pyramid was directly imaged. In 2025, researchers published a multimodal confirmation using ground-penetrating radar, ultrasonic testing and electrical resistivity tomography.

Four and a half millennia after construction, the architectural map is still being refined.

That fact alone should make us cautious about statements beginning with “we already know exactly what the pyramid is.”

The important point is not that a dramatic secret must exist.

It is almost the opposite.

The unknown can be real without our interpretation of it being correct.

Beneath Giza: Signal Is Not Structure

In 2025, dramatic claims spread internationally about enormous structures supposedly detected hundreds of metres beneath the Pyramid of Khafre using a satellite-based interpretation of synthetic aperture radar data.

The published visualizations were extraordinary: deep shafts, cylindrical forms and enormous geometric structures beneath the plateau.

They were also not an archaeological discovery in the established sense.

Radar specialists and Egyptologists challenged the physical ability of the method to resolve structures at the claimed depths, and no excavation or independent geophysical survey has confirmed the proposed underground architecture.

By 2026 the claim remained unverified.

This makes it useful for the article — not as evidence of a lost city, but as a demonstration of how easily a signal can become a story.

This sequence should become one of our rules for the entire investigation:

💡 KEY IDEA

Signal is not structure. Structure is not date. Date is not meaning.

The temptation is to jump from the first box to the last.

Archaeology exists precisely because we should not.

The Osireion: Architecture Below Time

If Giza confronts us with spaces we are still discovering, Abydos confronts us with something different.

The Osireion, behind the Temple of Seti I, is monumental, subterranean and visually austere. Massive granite elements surround a central architectural core associated with water. Its style feels radically different from the richly decorated temple nearby.

That difference has encouraged modern claims that the structure might be vastly older than Seti I.

The archaeological record does not currently support that conclusion.

Early excavators were themselves struck by the structure. Later work by Henri Frankfort connected the monument structurally and epigraphically with Seti I’s complex. The Egypt Exploration Society describes the Osireion as the enigmatic structure behind Seti’s temple, and the standard interpretation treats it as a cenotaph or symbolic tomb associated with Osiris and the royal funerary program.

The interesting question therefore is not:

Was the Osireion built by Atlantis?

There is no archaeological basis for stating that.

The better question is:

Why did New Kingdom Egyptians deliberately build a structure that evokes an architecture of primordial permanence?

Its subterranean character matters.

Its water symbolism matters.

Its monumental stonework matters.

And Abydos itself matters: by the Middle Kingdom it had become Egypt’s principal cult centre for Osiris.

The structure appears almost designed to make the visitor descend out of ordinary historical time.

Osiris and Reconstruction

There is a philosophical correspondence here worth making explicit — as interpretation, not archaeology.

Osiris is dismembered.

The fragments are gathered.

Order is reconstructed.

Something returns in another form.

The same pattern describes our relationship with ancient civilizations.

The monument survives.

Meaning fragments.

Every later civilization tries to assemble it again.

Hawara and the Memory of the Labyrinth

At Hawara, south of the pyramid of Amenemhat III, the situation is almost reversed.

Instead of an enormous monument surviving nearly intact, we have the memory of something extraordinary whose visible architecture was largely destroyed.

Ancient Greek authors described an Egyptian Labyrinth of remarkable scale. Modern archaeology identifies the principal mortuary temple of Amenemhat III at Hawara with that tradition. Petrie excavated the site in the nineteenth century, but found that much of the monumental complex had already been destroyed and quarried.

Yet the site did not become archaeologically empty.

A 2000 survey recovered additional evidence associated with the temple complex. A peer-reviewed 2010 geophysical study reported shallow elongated and square anomalies whose spatial distribution significantly matched aspects of the historical description.

A 2025 paper went further, interpreting satellite SAR imagery as possible evidence for a much larger buried structure.

That latest interpretation should be treated cautiously. Space-based radar claims about deeply buried architecture require independent validation, especially after the controversy surrounding similar claims at Giza.

But Hawara differs from the Khafre story in one important respect:

the Labyrinth is not invented by the modern scan.

Its historical and archaeological existence as Amenemhat III’s temple complex is already well established.

The open questions concern its original form, extent, surviving subsurface remains and how much of the ancient descriptions should be read literally.

The Initiatory Geography Hypothesis

Herodotus places the Labyrinth near Lake Moeris, in the Fayum region, not beneath Giza. The historical Labyrinth and the controversial structures recently claimed beneath the Giza plateau are therefore not the same archaeological claim.

Yet a later initiatory interpretation makes a different connection. In La pirámide iniciática, Joan Llarch asks whether a triple subterranean path could begin at the Sphinx, lead toward the three pyramids and continue toward the Labyrinth described by Herodotus.

This hypothesis directly echoes the reading developed in The Secret of the Sphinx, where the Sphinx is approached as a threshold to an initiatory journey through the Giza complex. Here, however, the question is widened: could that initiatory geography be not only symbolic and ritual, but also reflect a physical organization of space that is now only partially known?

This is not established archaeology, and it should not be presented as a geographical reading of Herodotus. It is better understood as an initiatory geography: the possibility that the Sphinx, the pyramids and the Labyrinth belonged to a larger ritual or symbolic system, whether or not a continuous physical tunnel ever existed.

That distinction allows three different kinds of connection to remain visible:

The physical connection remains unverified. The ritual and symbolic connection, however, can still be examined as an interpretive model: Sphinx as threshold, pyramids as stages of transformation, Labyrinth as ordeal, disorientation and reconstruction.

This does not collapse Hawara into Giza. It asks whether two geographically distinct places could have been understood, in later initiatory readings, as parts of the same sacred map.

Edgar Cayce and the Hall of Records

📚 CONTEXT

From this point, the article moves from an interpretive initiatory hypothesis into a visionary / esoteric tradition. The material that follows is historically important to modern Sphinx and Atlantis lore, but it is not archaeological evidence.

Joan Llarch imagines an initiatory geography. Edgar Cayce introduces a different kind of possibility: a repository of memory.

The distinction matters. Cayce’s material belongs to a psychic and esoteric tradition, not to archaeology. It should therefore be read as a modern visionary layer in the history of ideas surrounding Giza, rather than as evidence for an undiscovered chamber.

Yet the correspondence with the questions explored here is striking. In Cayce’s readings, the Sphinx becomes a sentinel associated with a sealed repository containing records of Atlantis and of the movements of its people. The Egyptian repository is described as connected with the Sphinx, while related records are also associated with Bimini/Poseidia and Yucatán.

The central idea is not simply that something was hidden. It is that knowledge was supposedly preserved for a later cycle — deliberately placed beyond the lifetime of the civilization that produced it.

That makes Cayce relevant to the theme of architecture for deep time even if his claims remain outside established archaeology:

  • Llarch asks whether a path of initiation could connect the Sphinx, the pyramids and the Labyrinth.
  • Cayce imagines the Sphinx as guardian of preserved records intended for a future rediscovery.
  • Archaeology asks what structures, passages and chronological relationships can actually be demonstrated.

All three approaches meet at the same threshold, but they are making different kinds of claims.

The attached 1968 volume Edgar Cayce on Atlantis, written by Edgar Evans Cayce under the editorship of Hugh Lynn Cayce, organizes the Atlantis material from Cayce’s life readings into a narrative of repeated destructions, migration, reincarnation and civilizational memory. Within that framework, Atlantis is less useful here as a historical conclusion than as a model of knowledge surviving collapse.

This also creates a useful progression across the two posts:

The Secret of the Sphinx — the Sphinx as threshold to a transformative journey.
Llarch — the threshold extended into an initiatory geography.
Cayce — the threshold extended into a repository of memory for another age.

The question therefore becomes broader than whether a literal Hall of Records exists:

What would a civilization choose to preserve if it believed its own world might not survive?

Before Egypt Was Egypt

The pyramids did not emerge from a cultural vacuum.

Predynastic Egypt extends thousands of years before the Fourth Dynasty, and archaeological material shows that the broader Giza area saw human activity before the construction of the great pyramids.

This matters because it changes a misleading binary:

either
Egypt invented everything suddenly

or
a lost civilization built Egypt

History does not require either extreme.

Knowledge can accumulate.

Techniques can be inherited.

Ritual forms can become monumental.

Older landscapes can acquire new meanings.

The more productive question is therefore:

How much of monumental Egypt was invention, and how much was culmination?

That question leaves room for continuity without requiring an unknown civilization.

It also leaves room for genuine surprise.

Archaeology repeatedly shows that what appears sudden at one scale can reveal long development when the scale is widened.

Atlantis: Answer or Archetype?

Atlantis should enter this discussion carefully.

Plato’s Atlantis is one of the most influential stories of a civilization destroyed by catastrophe. Through later interpretation it became a cultural container for a recurring human possibility:

a civilization before our civilization.

There is no accepted archaeological evidence showing that Atlantis built the Egyptian pyramids, the Osireion or the monuments of Giza.

So Atlantis should not be used here as an answer.

It is more useful as an archetype.

It asks what happens when:

  • knowledge outlives its institutions;
  • memory becomes myth;
  • landscapes are transformed;
  • civilizations inherit fragments whose origins they no longer fully know.

In that sense, the Atlantis question becomes larger than Atlantis itself.

Can knowledge cross a civilizational rupture without preserving the civilization that produced it?

Cayce’s Atlantis: cycles, migration and preserved memory

Cayce’s Atlantis material pushes that question to its extreme. In the readings as collected and interpreted by Edgar Evans Cayce, Atlantis passes through multiple periods of disruption before a final destruction, while groups disperse toward other regions. The material associates those migrations with Egypt and the Americas and repeatedly returns to a moral contrast between knowledge used for integration and knowledge used for domination.

None of this establishes Atlantis archaeologically. But within the intellectual architecture of this post it adds a revealing motif: civilization can disappear while fragments of its knowledge, symbols and moral warnings continue elsewhere.

Read this way, Cayce does not provide the answer to Egypt’s origins. He provides another modern expression of the same deep-time anxiety that surrounds megalithic monuments: the possibility that a civilization could try to send something through a rupture larger than itself.

Now the megalith returns to the centre of the story.

Built to Cross Ages

Imagine designing information for an audience you will never meet.

Language is unstable.

Political institutions are unstable.

Religions change.

Organic media decay.

Digital media, as our own civilization is beginning to discover, depend on extraordinarily fragile layers of infrastructure.

Stone is different.

Geometry is different.

The sky is different.

Together they form three unusually durable media.

Again, this is not evidence that the pyramids were intentionally designed as messages to a post-catastrophe civilization.

It is an observation about the medium.

A geometric relationship remains measurable even after the language used to describe it has disappeared.

A cardinal direction remains.

A celestial cycle can be rediscovered.

A stone can remain where it was placed.

This may be one reason monumental architecture so easily becomes a vessel for memory.

The monument as compressed civilization

A megalithic complex may contain, simultaneously:

engineering
geometry
astronomy
ritual
politics
labor organization
myth
landscape
religion
material science

The civilization disappears.

The monument remains as a compressed object.

Archaeology attempts to decompress it.

That metaphor is particularly useful because decompression is never guaranteed to recover the original file perfectly.

Some information survives.

Some correlations survive without explanation.

Some meaning is irretrievably lost.

And some of what we reconstruct may belong more to us than to the builders.

Time as the Audience

This leads to the question that separates this article from The Secret of the Sphinx.

That article asked about a possible legacy.

This one asks why the architecture itself seems so compatible with extreme duration.

Maybe permanence was simply the natural result of religious and royal ambition.

Maybe the purpose was to maintain cult, kingship and cosmic order indefinitely.

Maybe the monument was intended for the gods rather than for distant human observers.

These possibilities are historically grounded and should come first.

But once a structure survives thousands of years, something strange happens.

Its audience changes.

The builders are gone.

The ritual specialists are gone.

The original spoken explanations are gone.

The monument begins speaking to people who were never part of its culture.

At that point, time itself becomes part of the monument’s meaning.

Not necessarily because its builders consciously chose us.

But because they chose a form capable of reaching us.

What Have We Not Yet Learned to Read?

Modern archaeology has extraordinary instruments.

Muon detectors can reveal density anomalies through hundreds of metres of stone.

Radar can image shallow subsurface contrasts.

Electrical methods can infer resistivity.

Ultrasound can reveal internal structure.

Photogrammetry can preserve surfaces at extraordinary resolution.

AI can correlate datasets at scales that were impractical only a generation ago.

Yet better instruments do not automatically create better interpretation.

The hardest part remains the transition:

measurement
      ↓
structure
      ↓
date
      ↓
function
      ↓
meaning

The first stages increasingly belong to physics and engineering.

The last stages still require history, archaeology, language, comparative evidence and intellectual restraint.

Perhaps that is why Egypt remains so compelling.

We possess technologies the builders could never have imagined, yet the monuments can still place us in the position of beginners.

The message may not be hidden

We often imagine that the great discovery must be behind a wall.

Another chamber.

Another shaft.

Another room.

Another text.

Perhaps one day such a discovery will transform what we know.

But there is another possibility.

Perhaps the information is not hidden inside the monument. Perhaps the monument itself is the information.

Its material.

Its orientation.

Its relationship to landscape.

Its scale.

Its internal sequence.

Its relationship to death and regeneration.

Its resistance to time.

Its continued ability to generate questions.

The deepest unsolved problem may therefore not be another chamber beneath Egypt.

It may be the reading system required to understand what has been visible all along.

As Before, So After

The previous article used the old symbolic movement:

As Above, So Below.

This investigation suggests another axis.

As Before, So After.

The monument stands at the intersection.

Above and below.

Before and after.

Material and meaning.

Evidence and interpretation.

It survives precisely where these opposites meet.

And perhaps that is what makes megalithic Egypt so difficult to exhaust intellectually.

We assume the mystery is how the stones were moved.

That question matters.

But the stones also force another one.

Why choose a form that could remain after almost everything else was gone?

We may discover more chambers.

We may reconstruct more of Hawara.

We may understand the Osireion more completely.

We may find that some spectacular modern claims disappear under better measurement while quieter discoveries transform the field.

But the deepest question may survive all of them.

Why build as if time itself were part of the audience?

And perhaps the greatest discovery still waiting beneath Egypt is not another chamber.

It is learning how to read the monument.

References and Further Reading

  • Morishima et al. — Discovery of a big void in Khufu’s Pyramid by observation of cosmic-ray muons, Nature (2017)
  • Schumacher et al. — Confirmation of the ScanPyramids North Face Corridor using multimodal image fusion, Scientific Reports (2025)
  • Investigation of the North Face Corridor using Electrical Resistivity Tomography, Scientific Reports (2025)
  • AFP Fact Check — Scientists challenge claims of giant structures beneath the Egyptian pyramids (2025)
  • National Geographic — Is there really a secret city under Egypt’s Giza pyramids? (2025)
  • Egypt Exploration Society — The cemeteries and temples of Abydos
  • The Petrie Project — The Osireion at Abydos (1904)
  • UCL Digital Egypt — Abydos in the Middle Kingdom
  • UCL Digital Egypt — Hawara
  • UCL Petrie Museum — Hawara excavation and rediscovery
  • Uytterhoeven & Blom-Böer — New Light on the Egyptian Labyrinth: Evidence from a Survey at Hawara, Journal of Egyptian Archaeology (2002)
  • Khalil et al. — VLF-EM study for archaeological investigation of the labyrinth mortuary temple complex at Hawara, Near Surface Geophysics (2010)
  • Carlotto — Space-Based Ground Penetrating Radar Imaging of a Possible Underground Structure at Hawara (2025)
  • Joan Llarch — La pirámide iniciática (official book page)
  • Edgar Evans Cayce — Edgar Cayce on Atlantis (1968), documented in Edgar Cayce’s A.R.E. author archive — under the editorship of Hugh Lynn Cayce, Paperback Library / Association for Research and Enlightenment.

entry.title: AI Across the SDLC · Part 01 — Discovery & Product Planning

link.title: AI Across the SDLC · Part 01 — Discovery & Product Planning

entry.content:
Before AI helps us build better software, it should help us understand what should be built — and why.

In the introductory map for this series, the SDLC was presented as a lifecycle that can be progressively transformed by GitHub Copilot products, AI assets, knowledge, controls, and feedback loops. This first installment starts at the beginning: product discovery.

The practical challenge is simple, but foundational:

How do we transform scattered signals — interviews, support tickets, roadmap notes, existing documentation, and architecture constraints — into a clean, evidence-based understanding of what should happen next?

In this post, the running example is CaseFlow, a Rails-based product used to manage operational cases. The discovery topic is an apparently straightforward request: SLA-based escalation. The trick is that we do not want to jump directly from request to implementation. We first want product intent.

Contents

  • Why discovery matters in an AI-enabled SDLC
  • The first shift: initialize context only when needed
  • From signals to product intent
  • Evidence, inference, and unknowns
  • Discovery workflow in context
  • A simple lab with CaseFlow
  • Support material included in this package
  • References

Why discovery matters in an AI-enabled SDLC

It is tempting to think of AI as an implementation accelerator. But a weak understanding of the problem simply leads to faster mistakes.

Discovery is where we decide whether a request is:

  • a real problem,
  • a pattern across multiple signals,
  • aligned with product direction,
  • constrained by existing architecture,
  • or still too ambiguous to become backlog work.

That is why discovery is a strong place to begin introducing AI assets.

In this phase, the most relevant building blocks are:

  • Instructions — how the assistant should behave during discovery;
  • Discovery Skill — a reusable method for synthesizing signals;
  • Product Discovery Agent — a role-oriented way to analyze the problem;
  • Product Knowledge / early RAG — the relevant product context gathered from the repository and support materials;
  • MCP (optional) — useful if discovery must reach external tools or data sources.

The goal is not code. The goal is a discovery report that creates a reliable bridge to backlog shaping.

The first shift: initialize context only when needed

A practical pattern for this series is to introduce Copilot commands and shifts when they become useful.

Discovery is one of those moments.

Before asking the assistant to analyze a product request, it often helps to first improve its understanding of the repository and surrounding project context. In practice, that may mean using copilot init or an IDE-centered /init workflow if repository understanding still feels shallow or fragmented.

The principle is straightforward:

Use initialization when context is incomplete, not as a ritual.

In the CaseFlow example, repository context matters because discovery is not purely business-facing. The repository and support materials already contain clues about architecture, conventions, dependencies, constraints, and prior decisions.

A useful mental checklist after initialization is:

  • Does Copilot understand the repository structure?
  • Does it see the most relevant product and architecture documents?
  • Does it know the main conventions and recurring workflows?
  • Can it identify the parts of the product that matter to the current discovery topic?

If the answer is still weak, discovery analysis will also be weak.

From signals to product intent

For this first post, the CaseFlow request is: add SLA-based escalation.

At first glance, that sounds implementation-ready. But in discovery we are still answering questions like:

  • Is the underlying problem clearly stated?
  • What signals support the request?
  • Which product outcomes might it improve?
  • Which constraints or trade-offs already exist?
  • What should be clarified before backlog creation?

That is why “signals” matter.

Typical sources include:

  • customer interviews,
  • support tickets,
  • product vision,
  • roadmap notes,
  • existing documentation,
  • architecture decision records,
  • and current system context.

The point of AI in this phase is to connect those sources, not simply summarize them in isolation.

A useful output is product intent — a concise, evidence-based view of the problem, its context, and the most justified next step.

Evidence, inference, and unknowns

This is the most important intellectual discipline in the whole article.

Bad discovery often happens because conclusions are not labeled clearly enough. A team begins with vague signals, and then treats inference as fact.

A useful discovery workflow should always distinguish:

  • Observed / evidence — what the sources actually say;
  • Inference — what appears likely, and why;
  • Unknowns — what is still unclear and should block premature certainty.

This approach makes the discovery report far more trustworthy. It also makes later product and engineering conversations healthier, because assumptions remain visible instead of hiding inside apparently confident statements.

Discovery workflow in context

Once we step back, discovery becomes a coordination point between several layers:

  • product knowledge sources on the left,
  • GitHub Copilot products in the middle,
  • AI assets below,
  • and a cleaner product intent output on the right.

At this phase, GitHub Copilot can help through different surfaces:

  • Copilot in the IDE for focused exploration inside the repository;
  • Copilot Chat for questioning, reframing, and comparing findings;
  • GitHub Copilot CLI for structured investigation in a local project context;
  • GitHub Copilot App when broader workspace-level context helps discovery.

The key is not to use every product at once. It is to use the right surface for the kind of reasoning the moment requires.

A simple lab with CaseFlow

This package includes a small support lab around CaseFlow.

The discovery topic is SLA-based escalation. The support materials include:

  • product vision and roadmap,
  • personas,
  • synthetic customer interviews,
  • support tickets,
  • a feature request,
  • system overview,
  • ADRs,
  • discovery instructions,
  • a reusable Discovery Skill,
  • a Product Discovery Agent definition,
  • a discovery report template,
  • and a sample discovery report.

A good exercise is:

Ask Copilot to analyze the CaseFlow discovery materials and produce a discovery report for SLA-based escalation. The report must explicitly distinguish observed evidence, inferred insights, and unknowns.

A strong result should make it easy to answer:

  • Is the request justified?
  • What is already supported by evidence?
  • What remains unclear?
  • Should the next action be a user story, a spike, or a follow-up discovery step?

Choose the next move by the uncertainty left

  • User story

    Shape the request into backlog work when the problem and intended outcome are clear enough to act on.

  • Spike

    Investigate a consequential technical or product question that prevents reliable scope.

  • More discovery

    Gather or clarify evidence when the problem, its impact, or the product intent is still uncertain.

Support material included in this package

The complete companion lab is available as a downloadable package:

  • Download the Part 01 Discovery support package

It includes:

  • product vision, roadmap, and personas;
  • synthetic customer interviews, support tickets, and a feature request;
  • CaseFlow architecture notes and ADRs;
  • discovery instructions;
  • a reusable Discovery Skill;
  • a Product Discovery Agent;
  • exercises and suggested answers;
  • discovery-report template and sample answer.

The lab is intentionally lightweight. Its purpose is not to simulate an entire enterprise system yet, but to establish a repeatable discovery discipline that later posts can build on.
